content.content:
## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

....
## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.

The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
[Progress](#44-progress) describes.

### 5.2 Planner runs

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

### `libgit2/src/util/utf8.c` wave 232 batch 0: `git_utf8_char_length`'s `port/unexport`

The campaign's first later stage, forked from the working branch (`8f7af1223`): the export of
`fn::git_utf8_char_length` goes, with its raw binding and its allowlist entry, and its one C test
case leaves `c/`. Its port, `char_count`, keeps its API and its `Replaces` anchor. No C the
variants build calls it: its remaining callers, `fs_path.c`'s two sites, `fs_path.h`'s
`git_fs_path_validate_filesystem_with_suffix` and `tests/libgit2/refs/basic.c`'s
`test_refs_basic__longpaths`, are all under `GIT_WIN32`, which no variant defines, so the plan
counts no referrer. `utf8.rs`'s gateway keeps `git_utf8_iterate` and `git_utf8_valid_buf_length`
(waves 860 and 1531) and their signature checks. Its `unit_priv` tests lose their calls of the
removed export: `lengths_are_the_native_counts` becomes `prefix_is_the_native_prefix`, and
`empty_input_is_not_read` checks the two exports left. The module's and the gateway's docs no
longer name the export. `bindings.rs` was regenerated without the binding (`-22` lines), against
gen3, whose headers differ from gen4's only in the declaration the allowlist no longer reaches.

The C change is the fork's `9859ed5e7`, `unexport git_utf8_char_length`, on the local
`fork/main` after `c54c0c180`, not pushed; the superproject records it. It deletes
`tests/util/utf8.c`, whose only case is `test_utf8__char_length`, and removes the function's
declaration from `src/util/utf8.h`, a comment saying why in its place. The declaration went
because it no longer declares anything a build defines: an export serves only the remaining C
the target builds (the conventions' Exports section), and a header declares its module's
exports. A `GIT_WIN32` build of the fork would now meet the function undeclared at its four call
sites: under libgit2's default C90, an implicit-declaration warning (an error with
`ENABLE_WERROR` or a C99 compiler that refuses implicit declarations), then an undefined
reference to `git_utf8_char_length` at the link of `libgit2` and `libgit2_tests`. Had the
declaration stayed, it would have compiled and failed at the same link. Either way no Windows
binary links, as none did before, since no build of the campaign compiles that code; a port of
the Windows paths would call `char_count`. `tests/util/CMakeLists.txt` globs its sources, so no
CMake file changes. The spec ruled a later stage's C change out (`porting-workflow`'s Later
stages section), against `testing`'s carried-over cases, and said nothing of the declaration:
`crustify/evolution/later-stage-c-changes` proposes the rule, made on crustify's
`libgit2-crustify/evolution/later-stage-c-changes` (`86d8b2f`) and awaiting review.

The carried-over case: `char_count_carries_over_the_c_test` (`tests/unit_pub/src/util/utf8.rs`),
written by wave 229, holds `test_utf8__char_length`'s ten assertions with its inputs and counts
unchanged, each C string and size the bytes of one byte string, and names the case and its file,
as `testing`'s C tests carried over section asks. No assertion needed adapting, and none is left
uncarried. `test_refs_basic__longpaths` is compiled empty under the configured build, so it is out
of scope (the porting workflow's Tests follow their modules section) and is not carried over. The
`modules.json` record's `tests` still names `tests/util/utf8.c`, which is the plan's to correct.

their input. The gates that check it, and that the crate packages, are
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section's.

content.content:
## 4. Static inline functions

A `static inline` function a header defines is internal API of the module the
decomposition gives it, and is ported as its other functions are. Its C callers expand its
body in their own TUs, so an export alone does not reach them: at the module's
switch, the header's definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C
calls the Rust module's export, under the function's bare name, where it inlined the body.
<!-- TODO: cross-language LTO (`-Clinker-plugin-lto`, with a clang whose LLVM matches
rustc's) would inline the export back into its C callers. -->

## 5. Macros

A macro takes the Rust form [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section gives it,
which reaches the Rust items its expansion uses once they are ported. A macro a TU defines
goes with its TU. A macro a header defines, internal or public API that another module's C
may expand, also stays in its header for the remaining C, unexported, and its C and Rust
forms are not linked, beyond the Rust form's annotation. It keeps expanding where remaining C
invokes it, until its header goes with the last C file that includes it, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes: a type generator keeps minting the instances its remaining invocations define,
and what an expansion calls or accesses is reached as any remaining C reaches it, a
function or global Rust owns through its export, a type through its C layout. An
expansion site is a use by the function that holds it, so it holds back the later stages
of what it reaches, as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section counts its users.

## 4. Static inline functions

A `static inline` function a header defines is internal API of the module the
decomposition gives it, and is ported as its other functions are. Its C callers expand its
body in their own TUs, so an export alone does not reach them: at the module's
switch, the header's definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C
calls the Rust module's export, under the function's bare name, where it inlined the body.
<!-- TODO: cross-language LTO (`-Clinker-plugin-lto`, with a clang whose LLVM matches
rustc's) would inline the export back into its C callers. -->

## 5. Macros

A macro takes the Rust form [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section gives it,
which reaches the Rust items its expansion uses once they are ported. A macro a TU defines
goes with its TU. A macro a header defines, internal or public API that another module's C
may expand, also stays in its header for the remaining C, unexported, and its C and Rust
forms are not linked, beyond the Rust form's annotation. It keeps expanding where remaining C
invokes it, until its header goes with the last C file that includes it, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes: a type generator keeps minting the instances its remaining invocations define,
and what an expansion calls or accesses is reached as any remaining C reaches it, a
function or global Rust owns through its export, a type through its C layout. An
expansion site is a use by the function that holds it, so it holds back the later stages
of what it reaches, as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section counts its users.

content.content:
## 3. Batches

A wave's batches are packed when it starts, from the state of the campaign at that
moment, and packed again as its batches land or fail. Each batch holds items of one
objective and one route, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes
section describes: structs, unions, enums, typedefs and the macros that generate types,
or functions, globals, function pointers and the other macros. A foundational family's
allocator, releaser and cloner, which form one policy, share a batch.

A batch is sized so that its agent carries every item through its analysis, its tests and
its gates within one session, without its context running out, and so that what it lands
stays within what one review can follow. That size follows from:

- the items: a type's fields, its pointer fields above all, each of whose accessors
  follows from the analysis; a symbol's lines, its pointer parameters and returns, its
  function pointers and the type-erased values it hands on; and, in a foundational
  module, the lifecycle roles its items' strategies implement;
- the agent: its model, its context window and its effort;
- the campaign so far: which of the batches before it landed in one run, and which failed
  or ran out of context; and
- the host: how many agents run at once, as
  [`concurrency`](../../operations/concurrency/SKILL.md) describes, since fewer,
  larger batches share their analysis and more, smaller ones finish sooner.

The settings' `workload` answer, when it sets one, caps every batch: its types
(`max-types`), its symbols (`max-syms`) and their lines (`max-loc`).

Consecutive waves of a module, in index order, may share batches when every dependency
chain between their items stays within one batch: a batch that holds an item of a later
wave also holds every item of the earlier waves it depends on that has not landed. The
waves are folded so when they start, and the plan's order on disk stays as planned. Waves
that share batches land on the first one's integration branch, and are promoted
together.

An item that has landed is not packed again: an item a [wrap batch](#4-wrap-batches) bound
ahead of its consumer is dropped from its own wave in a wrap campaign, and keeps only its
`port` in a port campaign. A batch that fails may be packed again, its items into new
batches of its wave.

Review batches are packed the same way, from the landed batches they review, under the
`review-workload` caps when the settings set them, and larger than translation batches, as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s Review batches section
describes.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted

  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,

content.content:
# Goals

This file states what Crustify is for and how it evolves. Every change to Crustify is judged
against these goals, whether it changes its skills, its agents or its tools.

A rule that serves none of these goals is removed. Where two goals are in tension, they are
weighed for the case at hand, and the weighing is stated.

The goals evolve too, from the same evidence as everything else:

- a goal the campaigns keep missing;
- a goal no decision ever cites;
- two goals that keep conflicting the same way; or
- a well-founded change that none of the goals serves.

A change to the goals is proposed as Crustify's `evolution` skill describes. It lands only
with the user's approval.

Each goal names its *fitness*: what a campaign measures to tell how far the goal is met. Each
thing measured is a *measure*. A measure is read from one of two sources, and no run is made
only to take it:

- what the campaign's runs produce anyway: the dashboard, the review reports, the gates and
  the plan; or
- a rerun the campaign's reviews already make.

A *tier* is one of the checks that code meets one after another. An *escape* is a defect
caught by a later tier than the one that read the code first. Later tiers include:

- a module pass after a wave's review;
- a switch;
- a revisit; and
- a ship point's gates.

Worse work could improve some measures. Such a measure is *paired* with the measure that
catches the worse work, which is its *pair*, and neither is read alone. When there are more
escapes, fewer findings is no gain. When the work is redone, cheaper work is no gain.

Some measures are held by no artifact yet. Such a measure is marked **Not taken yet**. Until
it is taken, what it measures is judged, not measured.

Under each goal, **Measure** states a measure, **Paired with** names its pair, and **Not
taken yet** names what no artifact holds yet.

## 8. Incremental migration without breaking consumers

A codebase moves to Rust one module at a time. Every landing builds and passes its gates. No
consumer breaks: a C or Rust consumer's code does not change as what it consumes is wrapped,
ported or moves through its later stages.

- **Measure.**
  - The items whose API changed or went after their first landing, each with its reason.
  - The landed trees that failed a gate.
  - The target's test baseline, which moves only by the cases carried over.
- **Paired with** Idiomatic Rust's measure of C forms on the public API. An API that never
  changes because it stayed C's breaks no one and serves no one.

### The order

- **Measure.** The batches that met a dependency not yet landed, and waited for it, rewrote
  around it or reached past its wrapper.

  Items land after what they depend on. Where the order cuts a cycle, an item lands after
  the binding of what it depends on. That order is how this goal is met, and Safety's and
  Performance's with it: a consumer written once, over a boundary written once.
- **Not taken yet.** The whole measure.

## 9. Generality

The rules hold for any C codebase. What holds for one target alone is that target's lesson,
not a rule.

- **Measure.** Of what a campaign's evidence taught, the share stated as rules without the
  target's names against the share kept as the target's lessons. Also the rules a second
  target could not follow as written.

## 10. Least constraint

A rule states what must hold. Unless the how is itself what must hold, the rule leaves the
how to the agent.

- **Measure.** Per module, the rules that a run:
  - worked around;
  - rewrote sound code to satisfy; or
  - reported as forcing a worse result.
- **Paired with** what a loosened rule let through: the changes marked as weakening a check,
  and the defects found where a rule was loosened.

## 11. Consistency

One kind of item is translated one way. Items that mean the same in C take the same Rust
pattern, whatever their syntax and whichever agent, batch or campaign translates them. The
pattern is the one the conventions and the how-to skills give them. A departure states its
reason.

A pattern a skill gives is a how that must hold, in Least constraint's terms. A pattern is
given only where translating the same thing two ways costs a consumer or a reviewer. Where
the skills give none, the agent chooses. A choice met twice, where two ways would cost, is
proposed as the pattern rather than left to converge.

- **Measure.** The conventions findings reviews file, per item.
- **Paired with** two measures, since a review that reads less finds less:

# Goals

This file states what Crustify is for and how it evolves. Every change to Crustify is judged
against these goals, whether it changes its skills, its agents or its tools.

A rule that serves none of these goals is removed. Where two goals are in tension, they are
weighed for the case at hand, and the weighing is stated.

The goals evolve too, from the same evidence as everything else:

- a goal the campaigns keep missing;
- a goal no decision ever cites;
- two goals that keep conflicting the same way; or
- a well-founded change that none of the goals serves.

A change to the goals is proposed as Crustify's `evolution` skill describes. It lands only
with the user's approval.

Each goal names its *fitness*: what a campaign measures to tell how far the goal is met. Each
thing measured is a *measure*. A measure is read from one of two sources, and no run is made
only to take it:

- what the campaign's runs produce anyway: the dashboard, the review reports, the gates and
  the plan; or
- a rerun the campaign's reviews already make.

A *tier* is one of the checks that code meets one after another. An *escape* is a defect
caught by a later tier than the one that read the code first. Later tiers include:

- a module pass after a wave's review;
- a switch;
- a revisit; and
- a ship point's gates.

Worse work could improve some measures. Such a measure is *paired* with the measure that
catches the worse work, which is its *pair*, and neither is read alone. When there are more
escapes, fewer findings is no gain. When the work is redone, cheaper work is no gain.

Some measures are held by no artifact yet. Such a measure is marked **Not taken yet**. Until
it is taken, what it measures is judged, not measured.

Under each goal, **Measure** states a measure, **Paired with** names its pair, and **Not
taken yet** names what no artifact holds yet.

## 8. Incremental migration without breaking consumers

A codebase moves to Rust one module at a time. Every landing builds and passes its gates. No
consumer breaks: a C or Rust consumer's code does not change as what it consumes is wrapped,
ported or moves through its later stages.

- **Measure.**
  - The items whose API changed or went after their first landing, each with its reason.
  - The landed trees that failed a gate.
  - The target's test baseline, which moves only by the cases carried over.
- **Paired with** Idiomatic Rust's measure of C forms on the public API. An API that never
  changes because it stayed C's breaks no one and serves no one.

### The order

- **Measure.** The batches that met a dependency not yet landed, and waited for it, rewrote
  around it or reached past its wrapper.

  Items land after what they depend on. Where the order cuts a cycle, an item lands after
  the binding of what it depends on. That order is how this goal is met, and Safety's and
  Performance's with it: a consumer written once, over a boundary written once.
- **Not taken yet.** The whole measure.

## 9. Generality

The rules hold for any C codebase. What holds for one target alone is that target's lesson,
not a rule.

- **Measure.** Of what a campaign's evidence taught, the share stated as rules without the
  target's names against the share kept as the target's lessons. Also the rules a second
  target could not follow as written.

## 10. Least constraint

A rule states what must hold. Unless the how is itself what must hold, the rule leaves the
how to the agent.

- **Measure.** Per module, the rules that a run:
  - worked around;
  - rewrote sound code to satisfy; or
  - reported as forcing a worse result.
- **Paired with** what a loosened rule let through: the changes marked as weakening a check,
  and the defects found where a rule was loosened.

## 11. Consistency

One kind of item is translated one way. Items that mean the same in C take the same Rust
pattern, whatever their syntax and whichever agent, batch or campaign translates them. The
pattern is the one the conventions and the how-to skills give them. A departure states its
reason.

A pattern a skill gives is a how that must hold, in Least constraint's terms. A pattern is
given only where translating the same thing two ways costs a consumer or a reviewer. Where
the skills give none, the agent chooses. A choice met twice, where two ways would cost, is
proposed as the pattern rather than left to converge.

### `libgit2/src/util/utf8.c` wave 232 batch 1: review of wave 232 batch 0

The review of `wave-232/batch-0` (`d48feaced`), `fn::git_utf8_char_length`'s `port/unexport`,
for every objective, `fix` included, and the wave's gates. It files no finding and fills one test
gap.

The export's removal holds. The gateway keeps `git_utf8_iterate` and
`git_utf8_valid_buf_length` with their signature checks, and its `unit_priv` tests lose only the
calls of the removed export. `bindings.rs` loses the one binding the allowlist no longer reaches.
No Rust names the export any longer, outside the docs that say why it went. gen4's five variants
define no `git_utf8_char_length` in `libgit2.so`, and their `util_tests` list 53 suites, none of
them `utf8`. The fork's `fork/main` is `9859ed5e7`, which the submodule records.

Judged against the skills at crustify `cc84106`, the C change departs from `porting-workflow`'s
Later stages section, which has a later stage change no C. The test case's removal is what
`testing`'s C tests carried over section and `porting-workflow`'s Tests follow their modules
section ask of a `port/unexport`, so the skills conflict there, and
`crustify/evolution/later-stage-c-changes` is open on that. The declaration's removal is not in
the skills. It is consistent with the conventions' Exports section, since exports serve only
the remaining C the target builds, and with `porting-workflow`, which keeps a header for the
exports it declares. The four `GIT_WIN32` sites are:

- `fs_path.c`'s two sites;

  its `#else` branch; and

  section.

Without a definition, a `GIT_WIN32` build cannot link, declared or not. So the removal turns a
link failure no variant meets into a compile-time warning or error, and the review judges it no

**Verdict: rejected.** Two fixes are required. Both are contradictions with existing rules, and both can be fixed by removing text. Otherwise the change is sound: it answers the signal, sits in the right skills, names no target, touches no protected path, and **does not weaken a check**.

## Required fixes

1. **The new exception in `porting-workflow` Later stages leaves out the test harness.** The new text says a stage changes no C "but for" two listed things: the carried-over test cases and the header declaration. But `scheduling` §5.2 also has a `port/unexport` adapt the harness's own references to the export, or remove the harness. Eight scheduled items in this campaign have harness entries, for example wave 352's `git_trace_cb` in `deps/clar/clar_libgit2_trace.c`. Read as a complete list, the new text forbids an edit that `scheduling` requires.
   **Fix by removal:** end the sentence at "but for what still names the export a `port/unexport` removes" and drop the list after the colon. `testing`, `scheduling` and `porting-symbols` each already state their part. Adding the harness to the list would also work.
2. **`versioning` §5.5 Batches now contradicts the change.** It says a batch's `c/` is a submodule worktree at the recorded commit "since no batch changes the C". Under this change, a `port/unexport` batch does.
   **Fix by removal:** delete ", since no batch changes the C".

## Not required

- **Concurrent C commits (the gap most likely to come up).** Removing the declaration means nearly every function's `port/unexport` now changes `c/`. A wave can hold up to 23 such items, so batches in the same wave, or a switch integrating at the same time, will each commit on the fork's `main` from the same base. "As a switch's is" points to a procedure that is only safe because integrations run one at a time. The clash isn't silent: the batch that lands second hits a conflict on the `c` submodule commit when it rebases. Fixing this needs a new rule (for example, the fork's `main` moves under the wave's landing lock). Until then, task messages should say how to handle it.
- "Variants built from the C it leaves, as Builds describes for a switch": that section rebuilds the shared variants after landing. A stage batch needs its own private build, as `testing-builds` §1 says.
- Some existing wording now reads against later stages, though context makes the intent clear:
  - `porting-workflow` §3 says "A module's waves do not change the compiled target".
  - `versioning` §1 has the fork trimmed only by "the modules' switches".
  - "the stage's commit" should be "the batch's commit".
- The header-declaration and configured-out rules sit only in the Functions section. Globals inherit them through "as a function's does"; function pointers don't.
- Outside this diff: `porting-workflow` §1.2 already names `GIT_WIN32`, a target name, in the spec. It could be fixed by removing "such as `GIT_WIN32`".
- Problems in the proposal itself:
  - It names no goal or fitness measure, which `evolution` §4 requires. It serves goal 8, incremental migration (the baseline moves only by carried-over cases), and goal 10, least constraint (the run worked around the rule through its task message).
  - "Schedule records … carry `carries_over` cases, so every one of them changes `c/`" overstates. All 1783 `port/unexport` items have a record, but only 168 items (82 of 906 waves) list any cases. The conclusion still holds because of the declaration removal.
  - Its Status and Change sections name `86d8b2f`. The Record section explains that `0bec1f0` is the same skills diff, which I confirmed.
- The drafted record row is fine: a campaign can observe its recurrence signal, and `watched` is the right status.

## Evidence and validation

**Reran and confirmed:**
- gen3's plain variant defines `git_utf8_char_length` in `libgit2.so`, `git2`, `libgit2_tests` and `util_tests`. gen4 defines only `git_utf8_iterate` and `git_utf8_valid_buf_length`.
- `util_tests -l` lists 54 suites in gen3 and 53 in gen4, with no `utf8` suite in gen4.
- All four remaining call sites are inside `#ifdef GIT_WIN32`.
- The fork's `9859ed5e7` touches only `utf8.h` and `tests/util/utf8.c`.
- The run's task message granted the C change by hand, and the dashboard entries match the proposal.

**Not rerun:** the gen4 variant builds and the C test runs, which are expensive and whose outputs I checked above. A `GIT_WIN32` build isn't possible on this host, as the proposal says.

I changed, committed and landed nothing, and created no scratch files.
